summary: Children aged 7–8 learn to compare and group rocks by observable physical properties — hardness, texture (rough/smooth), colour, grain size, lustre (shiny/dull), and whether a rock crumbles. The central skill is choosing a property, sorting a collection by it, then RE-SORTING by a different property so learners discover that the same rocks group differently depending on the chosen criterion. Emphasis stays on evidence-based description ('this one is harder because it scratches that one') gathered with hands-on tests and hand lenses, and on observable properties rather than rock-type names (igneous/sedimentary come later): grouping precedes naming.
misconceptions: 'Rocks can only be sorted one right way' — not seeing that different properties give different valid groupings.
'All grey rocks are the same rock' — grouping by colour alone and ignoring texture/hardness.
'Bigger rocks are harder' — confusing size with hardness.
'You can tell a rock's properties just by looking' — skipping the test (scratch/rub) that gives evidence.

activities.title: Test, describe and sort a rock collection
steps: Examine a set of varied real rock specimens with a hand lens, looking closely at grain size and surface.

For each rock, carry out simple evidence-gathering tests: a scratch test for hardness (which rock scratches which), a rub test for texture (rough or smooth), a tap or gentle press to see whether it crumbles or holds together, and note colour and lustre (shiny or dull).
Record each rock's properties on a property card or a rock × property comparison table (hardness, colour, grain, texture).
Choose one property and sort the whole collection into groups (e.g. rough vs smooth, or hard vs crumbly), using sorting hoops/Venn hoops or a sorting mat.
Then re-sort the SAME rocks by a different property (e.g. switch from colour to hardness) and observe how the groups change.
State the evidence behind a comparison aloud, e.g. 'this one is harder because it scratched that one.'
activities.insight: A grouping depends on the property you choose: the same collection of rocks can fall into different groups when you sort by a different observable property, though some rocks may stay together. Describing rocks by tested evidence is more reliable than guessing by looking.

activities.title: Compare two contrasting rocks
steps: Take two clearly different rocks — for example one smooth, pale and crumbly, and one dark, heavy and very hard.
Describe how each differs across several properties: hardness, texture, colour, grain size and weight.
Decide and explain which group each rock would go into and why.
Answer: are all rocks basically the same, or can they be sorted into groups? Give evidence.
activities.insight: Rocks differ in several observable properties at once, so a single pair can be told apart and grouped in more than one way depending on which property you focus on.

activities.title: Is it really a rock?
steps: Look at everyday manufactured items alongside rock specimens (e.g. a brick, concrete, glass).
Decide whether each is a rock and give a reason.
Discuss what makes something a natural rock versus a material made by people.
activities.insight: Rocks are natural materials; bricks, concrete and manufactured glass (such as window or bottle glass) are made by people, often from rock materials, so they are not rocks even though they can be hard.

activities.title: Build observation vocabulary with a tap-to-reveal collection (supporting scaffold)
steps: Tap each specimen in a rock collection to reveal a property fact-card (hardness, texture, colour) and a lens zoom on the grain.
Use a lift-the-flap prompt: 'Which group would you put this in?' and choose a group before revealing.
Practise matching a rock to a property description and sequencing rocks by hardness.
activities.insight: Precise property vocabulary (hardness, texture, grain size, colour, lustre) lets you describe and compare rocks accurately.

checkQuestion: Here are two rocks: one is smooth, pale and crumbly; the other is dark, heavy and very hard. Are all rocks basically the same, or can we sort them into groups? What could you look at or test to describe and group them?
checkAnswer: Rocks are not all the same — they differ in observable properties, so we can group them. You can describe and sort by hardness (does it scratch easily?), texture (smooth or rough, grainy), colour, grain size and weight. Sorting by a chosen property puts similar rocks together.
